'''Charles Sheffield''' (25 June 1935 – 2 November 2002),<ref name=SFE/> was an English-born mathematician, physicist, and [[science-fiction]] writer who served as a President of the [[Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers of America]] and of the [[American Astronautical Society]].<ref>[[American Astronautical Society]] [http://astronautical.org/about/history/1974-to-present/ "History of AAS: 1974 to Present"]. Retrieved 4 June 2009.  {{webarchive |url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100718124531/http://astronautical.org/about/history/1974-to-present/ |date= 18 July 2010 }}</ref>

His novel ''[[The Web Between the Worlds]]'', featuring the construction of a [[space elevator]], was published almost simultaneously with [[Arthur C. Clarke]]'s novel on the subject, ''[[The Fountains of Paradise]]'' - a coincidence that amused them both.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sheffield |first=Charles |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/ocm45836846 |title=The web between the worlds |date=2001 |publisher=Baen Publishing Enterprises |others=Copyright Paperback Collection (Library of Congress) |isbn=978-0-671-31973-1 |location=Riverside, New York |oclc=ocm45836846}}</ref>  Excerpts from both Sheffield's ''[[The Web Between the Worlds]]'' and Clarke's ''[[The Fountains of Paradise]]'' have appeared recently in a space-elevator anthology, ''[[Towering Yarns]]''.<ref>
{{cite book
 |last1                = Clarke
 |first1               = Arthur
 |author-link1         = Arthur C. Clarke
 |last2                = Sheffield
 |first2               = Charles
 |author-link2         = Charles Sheffield
 |last3                = Crilley

 |date                 = 2017-12-22
 |title                = Towering Yarns: Space Elevator Short Stories
 |url                  = https://books.google.com/books?id=Mr7WswEACAAJ
 |series               = Volume 1 of Towering Yarns
 |publisher            = CreateSpace Independent Publishing Platform
 |isbn                 = 9781981495207
 |access-date          = 29 October 2022
}} 
</ref>

Sheffield served as Chief Scientist of [[Earth Satellite Corporation]], a company that processed [[remote-sensing]] satellite data.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Pace |first=Eric |date=2002-11-09 |title=Charles Sheffield, 67, Physicist And Author of Science Fiction |website=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/11/09/arts/charles-sheffield-67-physicist-and-author-of-science-fiction.html |access-date=November 15, 2024}}</ref>  The association gave rise to many technical papers and two popular non-fiction books, ''Earthwatch'' (1981) and ''Man on Earth'' (1983), both collections of false-colour and enhanced images of Earth from space.

He won the [[Nebula Award for Best Novelette|Nebula]] and [[Hugo Award for Best Novelette|Hugo]] awards for his 1993 novelette [[Georgia on My Mind (novelette)|"Georgia on My Mind"]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fantasy Writers Association |title=1993 Nebula Awards |url=https://nebulas.sfwa.org/award-year/1993/ |access-date=2024-11-16 |website=The Nebula Awards® |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2007-07-28 |title=1994 Hugo Awards |url=https://www.thehugoawards.org/hugo-history/1994-hugo-awards/ |access-date=2024-11-16 |website=The Hugo Award |language=en-US}}</ref> and the 1992 [[John W. Campbell Memorial Award for Best Science Fiction Novel]] for his 1992 novel ''[[Brother to Dragons]]''.<ref name=CA/>

Sheffield was [[Toastmaster]] at [[BucConeer]], the 1998 [[World Science Fiction Convention]] in [[Baltimore]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=56th World Science Fiction Convention - Bucconeer 1998 |url=http://209.68.15.119/ |access-date=2024-11-16 |website=209.68.15.119}}</ref> He was also a former President of [[Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers of America|Science Fiction and Fantasy Writes of America]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Present and Past SFWA Board & Officers |url=https://www.sfwa.org/prior-sfwa-board-officers/ |access-date=2024-11-16 |website=SFWA |language=en-US}}</ref>

Before he died, he was writing a column for the [[Baen Books]] web-site; his last column concerned the discovery of the brain tumor that led to his death.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sheffield |first=Charles |date=August 12, 2002 |title=Not My Favorite Column, Borderlands of Science |url=https://www.baen.com/Sheffield/Sheffield_Article.aspx?date=2002-08-12 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20021002093355/https://www.baen.com/Sheffield/Sheffield_Article.aspx?date=2002-08-12 |archive-date=October 2, 2002}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
{{More citations needed section|date=November 2024}}
Charles Sheffield attended [[St John's College, Cambridge]], where he graduated with a Double First in Mathematics and Physics.  During his studies he met and later married his first wife, Sarah Sanderson, whose death in 1977 became the catalyst for his writing career.  They had a son, Charles Christopher ("Kit"), and a daughter, Ann Elizabeth.  The family soon after moved to the United States, where Sheffield began working in the field of practical physics, a career that would lead him to a consultancy with NASA and the role of chief scientist at the [[Earth Satellite Corporation]] in Washington.<ref name=":0" />

In response to the traumatic grief from the death of his wife Sarah to cancer (in 1977), Sheffield began a second career as a  science fiction author,<ref name=":0" /> winning both the prestigious Nebula and Hugo awards and serving as President of the Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers of America (1984–1986). He maintained two successful careers, consulting for various scientific corporations while earning fame for his [[hard science fiction]].   During this period he lived in Washington, DC, and met and married [[Linda Zall]], a fellow scientist, and had two daughters, Elizabeth Rose and Victoria Jane.

At the time of his death, he was married to writer [[Nancy Kress]],<ref name=":0" /> and lived with his children in Silver Spring, Maryland.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2002-11-08 |title=Charles Sheffield 1935-2002 - SFWA News |url=https://www.sfwa.org/News/sheffield.htm |access-date=2024-11-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20021108105024/https://www.sfwa.org/News/sheffield.htm |archive-date=8 November 2002 }}</ref>

====''Waldo Burmeister and Henry Carver, Space Attorneys''====
Sheffield wrote about this series:
{{blockquote|In the late 1970s when I was just starting to write fiction, my young children (young back then, grown-ups now) ordered me to produce stories about every funny or disgusting thing in the world. They made the list for me. It had on it items of comic low appeal to them—sewage, visits to the dentist, mushrooms, fat aunts, opera singers, flatulence (I think they used a different word), comic Germans and Italians, fad diets, pigs, morticians, and head lice. Not an easy assignment, but I did my best. Over the years I have published ten politically incorrect stories tackling one or more of the listed topics... Together they form what I think of as my "sewage" series. They feature my two favourite lawyers, Henry Carver and Waldo Burmeister, and they are depressingly easy to write.<ref>Afterword to "Fifteen-Love on the Dead Man's Chest" in ''Georgia on My Mind and Other Places'', Tor 1995.</ref>}}
